lessons.title: Images and containers
lessons.summary: An image is a packaged filesystem and configuration; a container is a running or stopped instance created from it.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: An image is a packaged filesystem and configuration; a container is a running or stopped instance created from it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Containers add a writable layer and runtime settings such as mounts, limits and networks. Replacing a container does not change its source image. Persist required data outside the disposable writable layer.

lessons.takeaway: Containers add a writable layer and runtime settings such as mounts, limits and networks. Replacing a container does not change its source image. Persist required data outside the disposable writable layer.

lessons.title: Layering
lessons.summary: Image layers record filesystem changes and can be shared between images.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Image layers record filesystem changes and can be shared between images.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A later layer can hide a file without removing it from an earlier layer. Copying a secret and deleting it in a later instruction can leave the secret recoverable. Layer reuse reduces transfer and storage when content matches.

lessons.takeaway: A later layer can hide a file without removing it from an earlier layer. Copying a secret and deleting it in a later instruction can leave the secret recoverable. Layer reuse reduces transfer and storage when content matches.

lessons.title: Dockerfiles
lessons.summary: A Dockerfile describes build steps and default image metadata.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A Dockerfile describes build steps and default image metadata.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: FROM selects a base, RUN executes a build step, COPY adds files, and CMD or ENTRYPOINT defines startup behavior. Build-time and runtime environments differ. Pin dependencies and minimize unnecessary packages to make builds more predictable.

lessons.takeaway: FROM selects a base, RUN executes a build step, COPY adds files, and CMD or ENTRYPOINT defines startup behavior. Build-time and runtime environments differ. Pin dependencies and minimize unnecessary packages to make builds more predictable.

lessons.title: Build context
lessons.summary: The build context is the set of files available to a build.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The build context is the set of files available to a build.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: COPY paths are resolved within that context, and .dockerignore excludes unnecessary or sensitive files. A large context slows transfer and increases accidental disclosure risk. Keep credentials out of it and choose the intended context directory explicitly.

lessons.takeaway: COPY paths are resolved within that context, and .dockerignore excludes unnecessary or sensitive files. A large context slows transfer and increases accidental disclosure risk. Keep credentials out of it and choose the intended context directory explicitly.

lessons.title: Container logs
lessons.summary: Container logs expose output captured from the container's configured logging path, commonly stdout and stderr.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Container logs expose output captured from the container's configured logging path, commonly stdout and stderr.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Application logs written only inside the filesystem may not appear in docker logs. Logging drivers and retention determine availability. Correlate timestamps with restart and deployment history instead of assuming the latest lines describe the failure.

lessons.takeaway: Application logs written only inside the filesystem may not appear in docker logs. Logging drivers and retention determine availability. Correlate timestamps with restart and deployment history instead of assuming the latest lines describe the failure.

lessons.title: Port publishing
lessons.summary: Publishing maps a host address and port to a container port.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Publishing maps a host address and port to a container port.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The application must still listen on the correct address inside the container. EXPOSE documents a port but does not publish it. Binding a published port to loopback can restrict host-side reachability compared with all interfaces.

lessons.takeaway: The application must still listen on the correct address inside the container. EXPOSE documents a port but does not publish it. Binding a published port to loopback can restrict host-side reachability compared with all interfaces.

lessons.title: Volumes
lessons.summary: A Docker volume stores data independently of a particular container's writable layer.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A Docker volume stores data independently of a particular container's writable layer.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Mounting a volume at a path can obscure image content at that location. Container replacement preserves the volume unless it is separately removed. Backup consistency and ownership still depend on the application and filesystem.

lessons.takeaway: Mounting a volume at a path can obscure image content at that location. Container replacement preserves the volume unless it is separately removed. Backup consistency and ownership still depend on the application and filesystem.

lessons.title: Entrypoints
lessons.summary: ENTRYPOINT and CMD define how a container starts and which default arguments it receives.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: ENTRYPOINT and CMD define how a container starts and which default arguments it receives.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Exec-form startup passes signals more directly than a shell wrapper that does not exec its child. Runtime arguments can replace CMD or interact with ENTRYPOINT. Inspect the effective command when a container exits immediately.

lessons.takeaway: Exec-form startup passes signals more directly than a shell wrapper that does not exec its child. Runtime arguments can replace CMD or interact with ENTRYPOINT. Inspect the effective command when a container exits immediately.

lessons.title: PID one
lessons.summary: The first process in a container's PID namespace has init-like responsibilities.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The first process in a container's PID namespace has init-like responsibilities.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: It must handle termination appropriately and reap exited children it owns. An application or wrapper that ignores signals can delay shutdown until forced termination. A small init process can help with forwarding and reaping where needed.

lessons.takeaway: It must handle termination appropriately and reap exited children it owns. An application or wrapper that ignores signals can delay shutdown until forced termination. A small init process can help with forwarding and reaping where needed.

lessons.title: Health checks
lessons.summary: A container health check runs a configured probe to report application health separately from process existence.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A container health check runs a configured probe to report application health separately from process existence.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A process may be alive while its service is unusable. Probe interval, timeout and startup behavior affect detection. A Docker health status alone does not guarantee an automatic restart; the surrounding orchestration policy matters.

lessons.takeaway: A process may be alive while its service is unusable. Probe interval, timeout and startup behavior affect detection. A Docker health status alone does not guarantee an automatic restart; the surrounding orchestration policy matters.

lessons.title: User identity
lessons.summary: Container processes run with numeric user and group identities that influence file and kernel permissions.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Container processes run with numeric user and group identities that influence file and kernel permissions.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: An image USER instruction sets a default, but runtime configuration can override it. Host-mounted files retain host ownership semantics. Running as non-root reduces privilege but does not eliminate kernel or mount-related risks.

lessons.takeaway: An image USER instruction sets a default, but runtime configuration can override it. Host-mounted files retain host ownership semantics. Running as non-root reduces privilege but does not eliminate kernel or mount-related risks.

lessons.title: Memory limits
lessons.summary: A container memory limit constrains memory through kernel resource controls.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A container memory limit constrains memory through kernel resource controls.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The application may be killed when its cgroup cannot satisfy demand even if the host has free memory. Compare the limit with peak working set, cache and concurrency. Increasing the limit without understanding growth can move the failure to the host.

lessons.takeaway: The application may be killed when its cgroup cannot satisfy demand even if the host has free memory. Compare the limit with peak working set, cache and concurrency. Increasing the limit without understanding growth can move the failure to the host.

lessons.title: CPU quotas
lessons.summary: CPU quotas limit how much CPU time a container group can consume during a period.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: CPU quotas limit how much CPU time a container group can consume during a period.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Quota exhaustion can throttle runnable work and increase tail latency. CPU shares instead influence relative scheduling weight under contention. Inspect throttling and demand rather than interpreting an idle host as proof of adequate container CPU.

lessons.takeaway: Quota exhaustion can throttle runnable work and increase tail latency. CPU shares instead influence relative scheduling weight under contention. Inspect throttling and demand rather than interpreting an idle host as proof of adequate container CPU.

lessons.title: Bind mounts
lessons.summary: A bind mount exposes a specific host path inside a container.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A bind mount exposes a specific host path inside a container.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Changes may affect the host directly, and host path availability and ownership become deployment dependencies. A mount can obscure files packaged in the image. Use read-only mounts when writes are unnecessary and verify source paths carefully.

lessons.takeaway: Changes may affect the host directly, and host path availability and ownership become deployment dependencies. A mount can obscure files packaged in the image. Use read-only mounts when writes are unnecessary and verify source paths carefully.

lessons.title: Read-only filesystems
lessons.summary: A read-only root filesystem prevents writes to the container's root filesystem layer.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A read-only root filesystem prevents writes to the container's root filesystem layer.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Applications may still need explicitly writable paths for temporary files, sockets or durable data. Mount only those paths with appropriate storage. Read-only root does not make separately mounted volumes read-only.

lessons.takeaway: Applications may still need explicitly writable paths for temporary files, sockets or durable data. Mount only those paths with appropriate storage. Read-only root does not make separately mounted volumes read-only.

lessons.title: Multi-stage builds
lessons.summary: Multi-stage builds use several build stages and copy selected outputs into a final image.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Multi-stage builds use several build stages and copy selected outputs into a final image.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Compilers and build dependencies can remain in earlier stages while runtime artifacts go into a smaller final image. Copy only required files and verify runtime libraries are present. A smaller image is useful but not automatically secure.

lessons.takeaway: Compilers and build dependencies can remain in earlier stages while runtime artifacts go into a smaller final image. Copy only required files and verify runtime libraries are present. A smaller image is useful but not automatically secure.

lessons.title: Build cache
lessons.summary: The build cache reuses results when relevant build inputs have not changed.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The build cache reuses results when relevant build inputs have not changed.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Instruction ordering affects how much work must be repeated. Copy dependency manifests before frequently changing source where appropriate. A cached step may also preserve old package results, so dependency pinning and intentional refresh policy matter.

lessons.takeaway: Instruction ordering affects how much work must be repeated. Copy dependency manifests before frequently changing source where appropriate. A cached step may also preserve old package results, so dependency pinning and intentional refresh policy matter.

lessons.title: Secrets in builds
lessons.summary: Build secrets provide temporary sensitive inputs without intentionally baking them into image layers.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Build secrets provide temporary sensitive inputs without intentionally baking them into image layers.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Use the builder's secret mechanism rather than ARG, ENV or COPY for credentials. A build command can still leak a secret into output files or logs. Inspect resulting artifacts and keep secret use narrowly scoped.

lessons.takeaway: Use the builder's secret mechanism rather than ARG, ENV or COPY for credentials. A build command can still leak a secret into output files or logs. Inspect resulting artifacts and keep secret use narrowly scoped.

lessons.title: Image digests
lessons.summary: An image digest identifies content, while a tag is a mutable name pointing to an image.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: An image digest identifies content, while a tag is a mutable name pointing to an image.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Deploying by digest improves reproducibility and supports provenance checks. A multi-platform image index and a platform-specific manifest have different digests. Record what was actually deployed and use an update process for security fixes.

lessons.takeaway: Deploying by digest improves reproducibility and supports provenance checks. A multi-platform image index and a platform-specific manifest have different digests. Record what was actually deployed and use an update process for security fixes.

lessons.title: Networks
lessons.summary: Docker networks connect containers and provide scoped addressing and name resolution according to the network driver.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Docker networks connect containers and provide scoped addressing and name resolution according to the network driver.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: User-defined bridge networks support container-name resolution. Containers on different networks are not automatically mutually reachable. Host publishing and inter-container communication are separate paths with different controls.

lessons.takeaway: User-defined bridge networks support container-name resolution. Containers on different networks are not automatically mutually reachable. Host publishing and inter-container communication are separate paths with different controls.

lessons.title: Compose dependencies
lessons.summary: Compose defines related services, networks and volumes for an application.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Compose defines related services, networks and volumes for an application.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Dependency ordering alone does not guarantee application readiness. Health-based dependency conditions can help initial startup, while applications still need runtime retries and failure handling. Inspect the rendered configuration after variable substitution.

lessons.takeaway: Dependency ordering alone does not guarantee application readiness. Health-based dependency conditions can help initial startup, while applications still need runtime retries and failure handling. Inspect the rendered configuration after variable substitution.

lessons.title: Restart policy
lessons.summary: A restart policy determines when the runtime restarts a container after it exits.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A restart policy determines when the runtime restarts a container after it exits.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Restarting can recover transient failures but can also create a tight crash loop. It does not repair invalid configuration, missing data or an unhealthy process that never exits. Coordinate restart behavior with graceful shutdown and external orchestration.

lessons.takeaway: Restarting can recover transient failures but can also create a tight crash loop. It does not repair invalid configuration, missing data or an unhealthy process that never exits. Coordinate restart behavior with graceful shutdown and external orchestration.

lessons.title: Registry access
lessons.summary: A registry stores and distributes image manifests and layers.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A registry stores and distributes image manifests and layers.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Pull failures can arise from authentication, authorization, missing tags, network errors or rate limits. Verify the exact image reference and target platform before rebuilding. Keep registry credentials scoped and avoid embedding them in images.

lessons.takeaway: Pull failures can arise from authentication, authorization, missing tags, network errors or rate limits. Verify the exact image reference and target platform before rebuilding. Keep registry credentials scoped and avoid embedding them in images.

lessons.title: Resource cleanup
lessons.summary: Cleanup removes unused containers, images, build cache or volumes to reclaim space.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Cleanup removes unused containers, images, build cache or volumes to reclaim space.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Each resource type has different ownership and data-loss implications. Inspect usage and references before pruning; an unused volume may still hold valuable data. Avoid broad automated pruning without a documented retention policy.

lessons.takeaway: Each resource type has different ownership and data-loss implications. Inspect usage and references before pruning; an unused volume may still hold valuable data. Avoid broad automated pruning without a documented retention policy.

lessons.title: Socket exposure
lessons.summary: The Docker daemon socket exposes a control API with powerful host-level effects.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The Docker daemon socket exposes a control API with powerful host-level effects.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A process with access can often create privileged containers or mount host paths. Mounting the socket into an untrusted workload defeats many container boundaries. Treat daemon API access as privileged infrastructure access.

lessons.takeaway: A process with access can often create privileged containers or mount host paths. Mounting the socket into an untrusted workload defeats many container boundaries. Treat daemon API access as privileged infrastructure access.

lessons.title: Rootless mode
lessons.summary: Rootless Docker runs the daemon and containers without a root-owned daemon using user-namespace mechanisms.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Rootless Docker runs the daemon and containers without a root-owned daemon using user-namespace mechanisms.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: It reduces some host privilege exposure but has networking, storage and resource-control requirements. Check supported features for the environment. Rootless operation does not remove the need for image hygiene, least privilege and patching.

lessons.takeaway: It reduces some host privilege exposure but has networking, storage and resource-control requirements. Check supported features for the environment. Rootless operation does not remove the need for image hygiene, least privilege and patching.

lessons.title: Image scanning
lessons.summary: Image scanning identifies known vulnerabilities or policy findings in image contents.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Image scanning identifies known vulnerabilities or policy findings in image contents.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Results depend on package detection, advisory data and the actual deployed digest. Triage exploitability and exposure while maintaining update discipline. A clean scan does not prove the application is free of unknown vulnerabilities or unsafe configuration.

lessons.takeaway: Results depend on package detection, advisory data and the actual deployed digest. Triage exploitability and exposure while maintaining update discipline. A clean scan does not prove the application is free of unknown vulnerabilities or unsafe configuration.

lessons.title: Supply chain
lessons.summary: Container supply-chain controls establish where an image came from and how it was built.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Container supply-chain controls establish where an image came from and how it was built.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Pin inputs, record provenance, verify signatures according to policy and retain an SBOM where useful. Build and deploy identities need constrained permissions. Verification must cover the digest actually deployed, not merely a similarly named tag.

lessons.takeaway: Pin inputs, record provenance, verify signatures according to policy and retain an SBOM where useful. Build and deploy identities need constrained permissions. Verification must cover the digest actually deployed, not merely a similarly named tag.

lessons.title: Shared kernel
lessons.summary: Containers typically share the host kernel while isolating selected resource views.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Containers typically share the host kernel while isolating selected resource views.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A kernel defect can affect multiple containers and the host. Namespaces, cgroups, seccomp and privilege restrictions provide different layers of protection. Containers are not equivalent to independent virtual-machine kernels.

lessons.takeaway: A kernel defect can affect multiple containers and the host. Namespaces, cgroups, seccomp and privilege restrictions provide different layers of protection. Containers are not equivalent to independent virtual-machine kernels.

lessons.title: Stateful migration
lessons.summary: Stateful container migration moves an application together with compatible durable data.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: Stateful container migration moves an application together with compatible durable data.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Plan data consistency, schema compatibility, ownership and downtime before replacing containers. Copying a live data directory may not yield a valid database backup. Test restore and rollback with the application's supported procedures.

lessons.takeaway: Plan data consistency, schema compatibility, ownership and downtime before replacing containers. Copying a live data directory may not yield a valid database backup. Test restore and rollback with the application's supported procedures.

commands.title: List containers
commands.definition: Lists running and stopped containers.
commands.purpose: Find exited workloads and current image/port assignments.
commands.environment: Read-only; requires access to the intended daemon, which is privileged.
commands.expectedOutput: CONTAINER ID IMAGE COMMAND CREATED STATUS PORTS NAMES
commands.interpretation: STATUS shows running, exited or restarting; PORTS shows published mappings.
commands.safety: Read-only; requires access to the intended daemon, which is privileged.

commands.title: Inspect configuration
commands.definition: Returns detailed runtime configuration and state as JSON.
commands.purpose: Compare effective command, mounts, network and exit state with expectations.
commands.environment: Read-only but output can reveal environment secrets; replace CONTAINER.
commands.interpretation: State.ExitCode and State.Error describe termination; Mounts and NetworkSettings expose runtime wiring.
commands.safety: Read-only but output can reveal environment secrets; replace CONTAINER.

commands.title: Bounded logs
commands.definition: Reads a bounded recent set of captured container logs.
commands.purpose: Find startup and runtime errors near the incident.
commands.environment: Read-only; log driver support varies and output may contain secrets.
commands.interpretation: --since restricts time and --tail limits lines; use timestamps when correlation is needed.
commands.safety: Read-only; log driver support varies and output may contain secrets.

commands.title: Resource snapshot
commands.definition: Prints one resource-usage snapshot for running containers.
commands.purpose: Spot memory pressure, CPU usage and I/O differences.
commands.environment: Read-only; combine with historical metrics for capacity conclusions.
commands.expectedOutput: NAME CPU % MEM USAGE / LIMIT NET I/O BLOCK I/O
commands.interpretation: Compare MEM USAGE / LIMIT with configured constraints; a single sample can miss peaks.
commands.safety: Read-only; combine with historical metrics for capacity conclusions.

commands.title: Published ports
commands.definition: Lists container-port to host-address mappings.
commands.purpose: Confirm whether and where a service is published.
commands.environment: Read-only; publishing does not prove the application is listening.
commands.interpretation: 127.0.0.1 binds locally; 0.0.0.0 exposes all IPv4 host interfaces subject to other controls.
commands.safety: Read-only; publishing does not prove the application is listening.

commands.title: Network inspection
commands.definition: Displays a network's driver, addressing and connected endpoints.
commands.purpose: Check whether communicating containers share the intended network.
commands.environment: Read-only; inspect the intended daemon and network.
commands.interpretation: Containers lists endpoint attachments; IPAM describes configured address pools.
commands.safety: Read-only; inspect the intended daemon and network.

commands.title: Volume inspection
commands.definition: Displays volume metadata and driver configuration.
commands.purpose: Identify durable storage before replacing a container.
commands.environment: Read-only; never infer a volume is disposable from lack of a running container.
commands.interpretation: Mountpoint is daemon-host storage location for relevant drivers; Options may describe external storage.
commands.safety: Read-only; never infer a volume is disposable from lack of a running container.

commands.title: Storage accounting
commands.definition: Summarizes storage used by images, containers, volumes and cache.
commands.purpose: Locate the type of space growth before cleanup.
commands.environment: Read-only; do not automatically follow with prune, especially for volumes.
commands.interpretation: RECLAIMABLE estimates unused storage, not whether the data is valuable.
commands.safety: Read-only; do not automatically follow with prune, especially for volumes.

commands.title: Image metadata
commands.definition: Shows image configuration, identifiers and platform metadata.
commands.purpose: Verify the deployed image identity and startup defaults.
commands.environment: Read-only; metadata may contain build-time configuration.
commands.interpretation: RepoDigests identifies content references when available; Config contains entrypoint, command and user.
commands.safety: Read-only; metadata may contain build-time configuration.

commands.title: Render Compose model
commands.definition: Renders and validates the effective Compose configuration.
commands.purpose: Find variable substitution, merged-file and service-wiring mistakes.
commands.environment: Can expose interpolated secrets; requires the Compose plugin and the intended project files.
commands.interpretation: Read the resolved service settings rather than only source fragments.
commands.safety: Can expose interpolated secrets; requires the Compose plugin and the intended project files.

commands.title: Compose service state
commands.definition: Lists containers belonging to the current Compose project.
commands.purpose: Check missing, exited or unhealthy services together.
commands.environment: Read-only; project selection depends on directory and options.
commands.expectedOutput: NAME IMAGE SERVICE CREATED STATUS PORTS
commands.interpretation: State and Health are separate; absence may indicate the wrong project or uncreated service.
commands.safety: Read-only; project selection depends on directory and options.

commands.title: Daemon information
commands.definition: Reports daemon configuration, storage driver and runtime environment.
commands.purpose: Check rootless mode, platform and daemon-level differences.
commands.environment: Read-only; output contains host details and access to the daemon is privileged.
commands.interpretation: Compare Security Options, Docker Root Dir and driver fields with the expected host.
commands.safety: Read-only; output contains host details and access to the daemon is privileged.

commands.title: Client and server versions
commands.definition: Reports Docker client and daemon versions and API compatibility.
commands.purpose: Identify whether a command mismatch comes from the client or selected daemon.
commands.environment: Read-only; confirm the intended context before diagnosing a remote daemon.
commands.interpretation: Client and Server are distinct sections; a missing server section can indicate connection failure.
commands.safety: Read-only; confirm the intended context before diagnosing a remote daemon.

references.title: Client and server versions — primary documentation

commands.title: Context selection evidence
commands.definition: Lists configured Docker endpoints and the active context.
commands.purpose: Avoid inspecting or changing the wrong host.
commands.environment: Read-only; endpoint names alone do not prove environment ownership.
commands.interpretation: The asterisk marks the current context; Docker Endpoint identifies the daemon connection.
commands.safety: Read-only; endpoint names alone do not prove environment ownership.

commands.title: Image inventory
commands.definition: Lists local image references and recorded digests.
commands.purpose: Compare cached artifacts with the intended release identity.
commands.environment: Read-only; several tags can refer to one image.
commands.expectedOutput: REPOSITORY TAG DIGEST IMAGE ID CREATED SIZE
commands.interpretation: REPOSITORY and TAG are names; DIGEST is content identity when available and can be absent for local builds.
commands.safety: Read-only; several tags can refer to one image.

commands.title: Image layer history
commands.definition: Displays the image's layer history and build-command metadata.
commands.purpose: Investigate image growth or accidentally embedded build data.
commands.environment: Read-only but may reveal secrets embedded in old build arguments or instructions; protect output.
commands.expectedOutput: IMAGE CREATED CREATED BY SIZE COMMENT
commands.interpretation: CREATED BY describes recorded build instructions; SIZE is layer contribution, not necessarily unique disk usage.
commands.safety: Read-only but may reveal secrets embedded in old build arguments or instructions; protect output.

commands.title: Build a tagged image
commands.definition: Builds an image from the selected context and Dockerfile.
commands.purpose: Produce a repeatable candidate artifact from reviewed inputs.
commands.environment: Executes Dockerfile instructions and can use network/build resources. Review context exclusions and base images first.
commands.interpretation: Step output shows build stages and cache use; the final tag identifies the local result, not registry publication.
commands.safety: Executes Dockerfile instructions and can use network/build resources. Review context exclusions and base images first.

references.title: Build a tagged image — primary documentation

commands.title: Build with a secret mount
commands.definition: Makes a file available to BuildKit secret mounts during a build.
commands.purpose: Allow authenticated build steps without copying the credential into image layers.
commands.environment: Uses a local credential. Review Dockerfile handling, permissions and logs; never substitute ARG for a secret blindly.
commands.interpretation: The Dockerfile must consume the matching secret ID; a successful build does not prove application code avoided logging it.
commands.safety: Uses a local credential. Review Dockerfile handling, permissions and logs; never substitute ARG for a secret blindly.

references.title: Build with a secret mount — primary documentation

commands.title: Run an isolated local test
commands.definition: Starts a disposable container with one loopback-bound published port.
commands.purpose: Check a candidate service locally before deployment.
commands.environment: Runs image code and binds a local port. Use a trusted image and avoid production credentials/data.
commands.interpretation: The foreground output is application stdout/stderr; --rm removes this container after exit, not every external volume.
commands.safety: Runs image code and binds a local port. Use a trusted image and avoid production credentials/data.

references.title: Run an isolated local test — primary documentation

commands.title: Container process list
commands.definition: Displays processes running in a container from the daemon's perspective.
commands.purpose: Inspect wrappers and child processes without requiring ps inside the image.
commands.environment: Read-only; process arguments can reveal sensitive values.
commands.expectedOutput: UID PID PPID C STIME TTY TIME CMD
commands.interpretation: PID/PPID identify process relationships; displayed identifiers may correspond to host process IDs.
commands.safety: Read-only; process arguments can reveal sensitive values.

commands.title: Execute a diagnostic
commands.definition: Runs id in an already-running container.
commands.purpose: Check the identity used by an exec process in the container context.
commands.environment: The command is read-only, but exec permits arbitrary actions. Confirm container and avoid dumping secret environments.
commands.interpretation: uid, gid and groups describe this process; application processes may deliberately use different identities.
commands.safety: The command is read-only, but exec permits arbitrary actions. Confirm container and avoid dumping secret environments.

commands.title: Graceful container stop
commands.definition: Requests termination and allows a bounded grace period before forced stopping.
commands.purpose: Give a service time to drain and flush during an approved shutdown.
commands.environment: Stops a workload. Check availability, stop signal, data handling and restart expectations first.
commands.interpretation: The printed container name confirms completion of the stop operation; inspect exit state and application evidence.
commands.safety: Stops a workload. Check availability, stop signal, data handling and restart expectations first.

commands.title: Copy a diagnostic file
commands.definition: Copies a selected file from a container to the local filesystem.
commands.purpose: Preserve a scoped diagnostic artifact before container replacement.
commands.environment: Writes a local file and may expose confidential data. Choose a protected destination and a narrow path.
commands.interpretation: No output normally means the copy succeeded; inspect destination size and content separately.
commands.safety: Writes a local file and may expose confidential data. Choose a protected destination and a narrow path.

references.title: Copy a diagnostic file — primary documentation

commands.title: Filesystem changes
commands.definition: Lists paths changed in the container's writable layer.
commands.purpose: Investigate runtime modifications not represented in the image.
commands.environment: Read-only; this is not a full backup or a content diff.
commands.interpretation: A means added, C changed and D deleted; mounted-volume contents are outside this writable-layer diff.
commands.safety: Read-only; this is not a full backup or a content diff.

commands.title: Daemon event stream
commands.definition: Displays recent daemon events over a bounded interval ending now.
commands.purpose: Correlate starts, exits and health transitions with an incident.
commands.environment: Read-only event observation; daemon event history is not a durable audit archive.
commands.interpretation: Each event has a timestamp, object type, action and attributes; retained history may be limited.
commands.safety: Read-only event observation; daemon event history is not a durable audit archive.

commands.title: Network inventory
commands.definition: Lists networks known to the selected Docker daemon.
commands.purpose: Check intended bridge/network names before inspecting membership.
commands.environment: Read-only; inspect individual networks to see actual attached containers.
commands.interpretation: DRIVER identifies the network implementation; SCOPE describes its visibility.
commands.safety: Read-only; inspect individual networks to see actual attached containers.

commands.title: Volume inventory
commands.definition: Lists named volumes known to the daemon.
commands.purpose: Inventory persistent storage before deployment or cleanup.
commands.environment: Read-only; do not infer disposability from absence of a running container.
commands.interpretation: DRIVER and VOLUME NAME identify storage objects; a listed volume is not proof of a valid backup.
commands.safety: Read-only; do not infer disposability from absence of a running container.

commands.title: Compose bounded logs
commands.definition: Reads recent logs for one service in a Compose project.
commands.purpose: Investigate a startup failure without dumping every service's history.
commands.environment: Read-only; verify Compose project/files and protect secret-bearing output.
commands.interpretation: Prefixes identify service/container instances; --tail limits each container's retained lines.
commands.safety: Read-only; verify Compose project/files and protect secret-bearing output.

commands.title: Compose deployment
commands.definition: Creates or reconciles a selected Compose service and its required dependencies.
commands.purpose: Apply a reviewed local or single-host application configuration.
commands.environment: Mutates workloads and may recreate containers. Review resolved config, images, volumes and availability first.
commands.interpretation: Started or Recreated reports lifecycle changes; inspect health and application behavior afterward.
commands.safety: Mutates workloads and may recreate containers. Review resolved config, images, volumes and availability first.

commands.title: Export an image archive
commands.definition: Writes image layers and metadata to a local archive.
commands.purpose: Transfer a specific image to an approved offline environment.
commands.environment: Writes potentially large and sensitive image data; ensure adequate disk space and artifact access controls.
commands.interpretation: The archive is an image artifact, not a container data-volume backup. Verify its digest and destination size separately.
commands.safety: Writes potentially large and sensitive image data; ensure adequate disk space and artifact access controls.

debugging.title: Container exits immediately
debugging.symptom: A newly started container stops before serving traffic.

steps.evidence: Inspect exit code, effective entrypoint and logs. Check required environment, executable paths and architecture rather than repeatedly restarting.
Correct the image command or required runtime configuration and recreate from the reviewed image. If a deployment introduced the failure, use the known-compatible image as mitigation.
Confirm the container remains running, serves a real request and handles graceful stop correctly.

debugging.title: Published port still unreachable
debugging.symptom: A host port mapping exists but clients cannot connect.

steps.evidence: Compare the host bind address, container port and application's listener inside the container. EXPOSE alone does not publish a port.
Correct the mapping or application bind address and recreate with the intended limited exposure. Change firewall rules only if path evidence requires it.
Test from the intended client network and verify unintended networks do not gain access.

references.title: Published port still unreachable — primary documentation

debugging.title: Data disappears after replacement
debugging.symptom: Application data is missing after recreating a container.

steps.evidence: Determine whether data lived in the old writable layer, a different named volume or an unexpected bind source. Preserve the old container and volumes while investigating.
Recover from the correct retained data source or backup and mount durable storage explicitly. Correct deployment configuration so replacements reuse the intended data.
Create and read representative data across a controlled replacement and verify backup restoration separately.

references.title: Data disappears after replacement — primary documentation

debugging.title: Bind-mount permission failure
debugging.symptom: A non-root container cannot write to a mounted host directory.

steps.evidence: Compare the container UID/GID with host ownership, ACLs and security labeling. Confirm the mount is writable and points to the intended path.
Grant the application identity only the required rights or adjust ownership during provisioning. Avoid privileged mode or broad world-write permissions as shortcuts.
Test writes as the runtime identity and verify unrelated host paths remain inaccessible.

debugging.title: Memory-driven restart loop
debugging.symptom: The container repeatedly exits under peak traffic.

steps.evidence: Correlate memory growth with exit state, OOM evidence and configured limits. Distinguish a leak from a predictable concurrency peak.
Roll back a memory regression, bound concurrency or adjust justified capacity. A restart policy alone cannot fix insufficient memory.
Run representative load and confirm memory stabilizes and restart counts stop increasing without host pressure.

debugging.title: Compose starts before dependency ready
debugging.symptom: The web container fails on boot even though the database container was started first.

steps.evidence: Inspect dependency health and application connection errors. Start ordering is not proof of database readiness.
Add appropriate readiness handling and bounded application retries; use supported Compose health conditions for startup where useful.
Recreate in a safe environment and confirm startup succeeds with realistic database warm-up and later dependency restarts.

references.title: Compose starts before dependency ready — primary documentation

debugging.title: Unexpected old image
debugging.symptom: A deployment appears to use old behavior even after a tag was updated.

steps.evidence: Compare the running container's image ID with the expected digest and registry reference. A mutable tag and a locally cached image can diverge.
Pull and deploy the intended verified digest through the normal release process. Record digest-to-commit mapping instead of relying only on tag names.
Inspect the running container identity and verify the expected feature and rollback artifact.

debugging.title: Container ignores shutdown
debugging.symptom: Stopping a container waits for the timeout and then forces termination.

steps.evidence: Inspect PID-one behavior and shell wrappers; determine whether signals reach the application and whether it drains work.
Use exec-form startup or a suitable init/wrapper that forwards signals and reaps children. Implement bounded graceful shutdown in the application.
Send a controlled stop during test work and verify graceful exit, completed or safely retried requests and no zombie buildup.

debugging.title: Host storage consumed by Docker
debugging.symptom: The daemon host is running out of disk space.

steps.evidence: Separate image/cache growth from container logs and durable volumes. Identify owners and retention before deleting any resource.
Apply scoped cleanup to confirmed disposable resources and configure log/cache retention. Do not prune volumes just because they are currently detached.
Confirm reclaimed space and successful application data access; monitor growth after the next build and log cycle.

references.title: Host storage consumed by Docker — primary documentation

debugging.title: Secret accidentally baked into image
debugging.symptom: A credential was copied during build and deleted in a later Dockerfile step.

steps.evidence: Inspect the build process and layer history; later deletion does not remove earlier layer contents. Assess registry and artifact access.
Rotate the exposed credential, rebuild without the secret using a proper secret mechanism and remove affected artifacts under policy.
Verify the replacement image and build logs contain no secret material and consumers use the rotated credential.

references.title: Secret accidentally baked into image — primary documentation
